title: Needle-felted long-tailed tit
subtitle: A tiny pink-white-and-black bird with a tail longer than its body
excerpt: Needle felt a long-tailed tit in white and pale pink merino with a black shoulder stripe and that distinctive long, narrow tail. The body is barely 3 cm; the tail adds another 7 cm. Wire inside the tail stops it drooping.
sourceNotes: Synthesised from traditional British needle-felting guild practice. The long-tailed tit is a popular British garden bird form used in beginner and intermediate workshops.

glossaryTerms.definition: A dry felting method using barbed needles to lock wool fibres together without heat or water.
A wire frame inside a needle-felted piece, used to allow fine elements like tails and limbs to be shaped and held in position.
Wool drawn into a continuous ribbon; the standard input material for needle-felting.

attrs.title: Needle safety
attrs.body: Stab straight in and out at 90 degrees. At this small scale, fingers are very close to the needle tip; use the finger guard throughout.

items.name: Thin wire (0.4 mm florists or craft wire)
Strong thread and needle for bead eyes

content.text: Roll a small amount of white roving into a compact ball about 2.5 cm across when firm. Needle felt on all sides. The body is round and almost spherical. Roll a slightly smaller ball for the head and needle it firmly onto the front of the body. The neck is almost non-existent in the long-tailed tit; head and body sit close together.

Needle a thin stripe of black roving along each shoulder, running from the base of the bill back over the head and down each side of the back. The stripe is narrow (about 3 mm) and sits above the wing area. Add a pale pink flush to the breast and belly by needling a thin layer of pink roving over the white. Shape a short, pointed bill from dark grey roving.

Take a 10 cm length of wire and wrap it tightly along its length with a thin strip of black roving. Needle the roving wrapping into the wire until the surface is smooth and the wire is covered. Bend the last centimetre of wire into a small hook to act as a grip point when attaching it to the body. The tail should be about 7 cm of the wire; the remaining 3 cm hooks into the body.

Push the hooked end of the wire tail into the back of the body and needle the surrounding roving over the insertion point to secure it. Apply a small additional layer of white or black roving at the join and needle it smooth. Bend the tail into the characteristic slight upward curve of the live bird. Needle thin white edges along each side of the tail to suggest the outer white tail feathers.

Stitch the bead eyes into the head, one on each side just behind the bill. Long-tailed tits have a prominent white eye-ring; you can suggest this by needling a tiny ring of white roving around each bead after stitching. Trim any loose fibres.

items.problem: The wire tail droops under its own weight
items.cause: The roving wrap was too loose on the wire, giving it no stiffness
items.fix: Wrap the roving tightly before needling; the needle-felted wrapping adds very little structural stiffness, so the tightness of the wrap itself matters. A slightly thicker wire also helps.

items.problem: The black shoulder stripe is too wide
items.cause: Too much black roving was applied, or it spread during needling
items.fix: Remove surface fibres with a fine needle point and re-needle a thin strip. The stripe should be about 3 mm at its widest; anything wider makes the bird look dirty rather than marked.
